title: Where 'Benevolent Dictator for Life' Comes From (1995)
explainer: The tongue-in-cheek title 'Benevolent Dictator for Life' (BDFL), used for open-source leaders who hold final say over a project's direction, traces to 1995 and the early Python mailing list: core contributor Ken Manheimer proposed calling Guido van Rossum the project's 'Benevolent Dictator,' and fellow contributor Barry Warsaw added 'for Life' shortly after. Van Rossum held the title for over two decades, until he stepped back from it in 2018. The title's staying power says something real about open-source governance: technical authority and community trust, not an org chart, are what make a project leader's calls carry weight.

title: The Open Source Definition and the Founding of the OSI (1998)
explainer: In February 1998, Bruce Perens and Eric Raymond founded the Open Source Initiative and adapted Perens's earlier Debian Free Software Guidelines into the Open Source Definition, the ten-criteria standard still used to decide whether a license counts as 'open source.' The move was a deliberate branding and governance choice, distinct from the older free-software movement, aimed at making open collaboration sound pragmatic and business-friendly rather than purely ideological. For anyone stepping into an open-source leadership role, it is worth knowing that the category you are operating in - what licenses, contributions, and governance structures count as legitimately 'open' - was settled by a small group making contested choices, not handed down by consensus.
